paragraphs: Resuming the subject of the last paper, I proceed to inquire whether the federal government or the State governments will have the advantage with regard to the preference and support of the people. The two are appointed in different ways, but we must consider both of them as substantially dependent on the great body of the citizens of the United States. I assume this position here as it concerns the federal government, reserving the proofs for another place. The federal and State governments are in fact only different agents and trustees of the people, constituted with different powers and designed for different purposes. The opponents of the Constitution seem to have lost sight of the people altogether in their reasoning on this subject. They seem to have viewed these different establishments not only as mutual rivals and enemies but as free of any common superior in their efforts to usurp each other's authorities. These gentlemen must here be reminded of their error. They must be told that the ultimate authority, wherever the derivative authority may be found, resides in the people alone. Whether either government, or which of them, will be able to enlarge its sphere of jurisdiction at the expense of the other will not depend merely on the comparative ambition or skill of the different governments. Truth, no less than decency, requires that in every case the outcome be supposed to depend on the views and sanction of their common constituents.

Many considerations, besides those suggested on a former occasion, seem to place it beyond doubt that the first and most natural attachment of the people will be to the governments of their respective States. A greater number of individuals will expect to rise into the administration of these governments. From their gift a greater number of offices and emoluments will flow. By their watchful care, all the more domestic and personal interests of the people will be regulated and provided for. The people will be more familiar with their affairs, and more minutely acquainted with them. And a greater proportion of the people will have ties of personal acquaintance and friendship, and of family and party attachment, with their members. On the side of these governments, therefore, the popular bias may well be expected to incline most strongly.

Experience speaks the same language in this case. The federal administration has so far been very defective in comparison with what may be hoped for under a better system. Yet during the war, and particularly while the independent fund of paper emissions was in credit, it had as much activity and importance as it can well have in any future circumstances whatever. It was engaged, too, in a course of measures whose object was the protection of everything dear to the people at large and the acquisition of everything that could be desirable to them. It was nevertheless invariably found, after the passing enthusiasm for the early Congresses was over, that the attention and attachment of the people turned again to their own particular governments. The federal council was at no time the idol of popular favor. And opposition to proposed enlargements of its powers and importance was usually the side taken by the men who wished to build their political consequence on the prepossessions of their fellow citizens.

If, therefore, as has been remarked elsewhere, the people should in future become more biased toward the federal government than toward the State governments, the change can only result from such manifest and irresistible proofs of better administration as will overcome all their earlier inclinations. In that case the people surely ought not to be prevented from giving most of their confidence where they find it to be most due. But even in that case the State governments would have little to fear, because the federal power can, in the nature of things, be administered advantageously only within a certain sphere.
The remaining points on which I propose to compare the federal and State governments are the disposition and the ability each may have to resist and frustrate the measures of the other.

It has already been proved that the members of the federal government will be more dependent on the members of the State governments than the latter will be on the former. It has also appeared that the prepossessions of the people, on whom both will depend, will be more on the side of the State governments than of the federal government. As far as the disposition of each toward the other may be influenced by these causes, the State governments must clearly have the advantage. But from a distinct and very important point of view, the advantage will lie on the same side. The prepossessions which the members themselves will carry into the federal government will generally be favorable to the States. It will rarely happen that the members of the State governments carry into the public councils a bias in favor of the general government. A local spirit will infallibly prevail much more in the members of Congress than a national spirit will prevail in the legislatures of the particular States. Everyone knows that a great proportion of the errors committed by the State legislatures comes from the disposition of the members to sacrifice the comprehensive and permanent interest of the State to the particular and separate views of the counties or districts where they live. And if they do not sufficiently enlarge their policy to embrace the collective welfare of their particular State, how can it be imagined that they will make the aggregate prosperity of the Union, and the dignity and respectability of its government, the objects of their affections and deliberations? For the same reason that the members of the State legislatures will be unlikely to attach themselves sufficiently to national objects, the members of the federal legislature will be likely to attach themselves too much to local objects. The States will be to the latter what counties and towns are to the former. Measures will too often be decided according to their probable effect, not on the national prosperity and happiness, but on the prejudices, interests, and pursuits of the governments and people of the individual States. What has been the spirit that has in general characterized the proceedings of Congress? A reading of their journals, as well as the frank acknowledgments of those who have had a seat in that assembly, will tell us that the members have too frequently shown the character of partisans of their respective States rather than of impartial guardians of a common interest. On one occasion improper sacrifices have been made of local considerations to the aggrandizement of the federal government, but on a hundred the great interests of the nation have suffered from undue attention to the local prejudices, interests, and views of the particular States. I do not mean by these reflections to insinuate that the new federal government will not embrace a more enlarged plan of policy than the existing government has pursued. Much less do I mean that its views will be as confined as those of the State legislatures. I mean only that it will partake sufficiently of the spirit of both to be disinclined to invade the rights of the individual States or the prerogatives of their governments. The motives on the part of the State governments to augment their prerogatives by subtractions from the federal government will be overruled by no reciprocal predispositions in the members.

Were it admitted, however, that the federal government may feel as much disposition as the State governments to extend its power beyond the due limits, the latter would still have the advantage in the means of defeating such encroachments. Suppose an act of a particular State, though unfriendly to the national government, is generally popular in that State and does not too grossly violate the oaths of the State officers. It is executed immediately and, of course, by means on the spot and depending on the State alone. Opposition from the federal government, or the interposition of federal officers, would only inflame the zeal of all parties on the side of the State. The evil could not be prevented or repaired, if at all, without the use of means which must always be resorted to with reluctance and difficulty. On the other hand, suppose an unwarrantable measure of the federal government is unpopular in particular States, which would seldom fail to be the case. Or suppose even a warrantable measure is unpopular, which may sometimes be the case. The means of opposition to it are then powerful and at hand. The disquiet of the people; their repugnance and, perhaps, refusal to cooperate with the officers of the Union; the frowns of the State's chief executive; the embarrassments created by legislative devices, which would often be added on such occasions: these would present, in any State, difficulties not to be despised. In a large State they would form very serious impediments. And where the views of several adjoining States happened to be in unison, they would present obstructions which the federal government would hardly be willing to encounter.

But ambitious encroachments by the federal government on the authority of the State governments would not excite the opposition of a single State, or of a few States only. They would be signals of general alarm. Every government would take up the common cause. A correspondence would be opened. Plans of resistance would be concerted. One spirit would animate and conduct the whole. The same combinations, in short, would result from the apprehension of a federal yoke as were produced by the dread of a foreign one. And unless the projected innovations were voluntarily renounced, the same appeal to a trial of force would be made in the one case as was made in the other. But what degree of madness could ever drive the federal government to such an extremity? In the contest with Great Britain, one part of the empire was employed against the other. The more numerous part invaded the rights of the less numerous part. The attempt was unjust and unwise, but in theory it was not absolutely chimerical. But what would the contest be in the case we are supposing? Who would be the parties? A few representatives of the people would be opposed to the people themselves. Or rather, one set of representatives would be contending against thirteen sets of representatives, with the whole body of their common constituents on the side of the latter.

The only refuge left to those who prophesy the downfall of the State governments is the visionary supposition that the federal government may first accumulate a military force for the projects of ambition. The reasonings contained in these papers must have been employed to little purpose indeed if it is now necessary to disprove the reality of this danger. Consider what the supposition requires. The people and the States would have to elect, for a sufficient period of time, an uninterrupted succession of men ready to betray both. The traitors would have to pursue, uniformly and systematically throughout this period, some fixed plan for the extension of the military establishment. And the governments and the people of the States would have to watch the gathering storm silently and patiently, and keep supplying the materials, until it was ready to burst on their own heads. This must appear to everyone more like the incoherent dreams of a delirious jealousy, or the misjudged exaggerations of a counterfeit zeal, than like the sober apprehensions of genuine patriotism. Extravagant as the supposition is, however, let it be made. Let a regular army fully equal to the resources of the country be formed, and let it be entirely at the devotion of the federal government. Still it would not be going too far to say that the State governments, with the people on their side, would be able to repel the danger. By the best computation, the highest number to which a standing army can be carried in any country does not exceed one hundredth part of the whole number of souls, or one twenty-fifth part of the number able to bear arms. In the United States this proportion would not yield an army of more than twenty-five or thirty thousand men. To these would be opposed a militia amounting to nearly half a million citizens with arms in their hands, officered by men chosen from among themselves, fighting for their common liberties, and united and led by governments possessing their affections and confidence. It may well be doubted whether a militia thus circumstanced could ever be conquered by such a proportion of regular troops. Those who are best acquainted with the recent successful resistance of this country against the British arms will be most inclined to deny the possibility of it. The Americans possess the advantage of being armed, which they have over the people of almost every other nation. Besides that, there is the existence of subordinate governments, to which the people are attached and by which the militia officers are appointed. This forms a barrier against the enterprises of ambition more insurmountable than any that a simple government of any form can admit of. The several kingdoms of Europe carry their military establishments as far as the public resources will bear, and yet their governments are afraid to trust the people with arms. And it is not certain that, with arms alone, the people would not be able to shake off their yokes. But suppose the people possessed the additional advantages of local governments chosen by themselves, which could collect the national will and direct the national force, and of officers appointed out of the militia by these governments and attached both to them and to the militia. It may be affirmed with the greatest assurance that the throne of every tyranny in Europe would be speedily overturned in spite of the legions that surround it. Let us not insult the free and gallant citizens of America with the suspicion that they would be less able to defend the rights they actually possess than the debased subjects of arbitrary power would be to rescue theirs from the hands of their oppressors. Let us rather no longer insult them with the supposition that they can ever reduce themselves to the necessity of making the experiment, by a blind and tame submission to the long train of insidious measures which must precede and produce it.

The argument under the present head may be put into a very concise form, which appears altogether conclusive. Either the way the federal government is to be constructed will make it sufficiently dependent on the people, or it will not. On the first supposition, that dependence will restrain it from forming schemes obnoxious to its constituents. On the other supposition, it will not possess the confidence of the people, and its schemes of usurpation will be easily defeated by the State governments, which will be supported by the people.

Summing up the considerations stated in this and the last paper, they seem to amount to the most convincing evidence that the powers proposed to be lodged in the federal government are as little formidable to those reserved to the individual States as they are indispensably necessary to accomplish the purposes of the Union. And all those alarms which have been sounded, of a meditated and consequent annihilation of the State governments, must, on the most favorable interpretation, be ascribed to the chimerical fears of the authors of them.
